title: A Warped Born Rule Turns an Observer into a Maxwell's Demon
abstract: Quantum mechanics seems to be an incredibly delicate theory. Slight alterations to nearly any part of its structure can lead to huge qualitative differences and wildly unphysical predictions. Here, we explore the many-body consequences of replacing the Born rule $p(m)\propto\|P_m|ψ\rangle|^2$ by a warped rule $p_b(m)\propto\|P_m|ψ\rangle\|^{2b}$. Specifically, in systems with conserved particle number, evolution punctuated by repeated local particle observations acquires a probabilistic bias over measurement histories with an effect controlled by the sign of $b-1$. For $b>1$, this bias generically drives the gas to collect into nearly frozen configurations. Similar to the action of Maxwell's demon, the simple act of observation seems to extract entropy from a closed system. For $b<1$, the bias is reversed, generically scouring out long-wavelength fluctuations to produce a hyperuniform gas. We study this effect in a one-dimensional quantum gas, where these two phases are derived analytically for a particular measurement scheme and corroborated numerically for more general procedures with discrete-time projective-measurement circuit models using matrix product state simulations. We additionally discuss how this bias manifests in a common technique that often employs this warped rule, the ``replica trick,'' implying qualitative differences between finite-replica and replica-limit calculations.
summary: This work explores how modifying the Born rule in quantum measurements introduces a systematic bias into the system's evolution. This bias causes the quantum gas to either cluster into dense, frozen states ($b>1$) or become highly uniform (hyperuniform, $b<1$). The findings suggest that the act of observation itself can act as an engine for entropy change, analogous to Maxwell's Demon.
main_problem: The paper investigates the many-body consequences of replacing the standard Born rule in quantum measurements with a warped rule, $p_b(m) \propto \lVert P_m|\psiangleVert^{2b}$. This modification introduces a probabilistic bias over measurement histories.
main_result: The bias dictates the system's long-term state: $b>1$ drives the gas toward clustering (entropy extraction, like Maxwell's demon), while $b<1$ suppresses long-wavelength fluctuations, leading to a hyperuniform gas.
method: The analysis uses information theory, comparing the warped rule to the standard Born rule, and employs numerical simulations like Matrix Product States (MPS) to study the resulting phase selection in 1D quantum gases.
model_or_system: The study models a diffusing quantum gas with conserved particle number, analyzed in 1D. The dynamics are related to an activity-biased Symmetric Exclusion Process (SEP) when considering the continuous-time limit.
key_observables: Structure factors $S(q)$, local polarization $M_2(t)$, and the bias parameter $b$.
important_parameters: The bias parameter $b$, which controls the sign of the entropic bias ($b-1$). Regimes include $b>1$ (clustering) and $b<1$ (hyperuniformity).
main_assumptions: The analysis distinguishes between global and sequential normalization procedures, and the connection to solvable classical models (SEP) is used to guide the understanding of the quantum bias.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the physical effect of the bias, showing particle collection for $b>1$ and suppression of fluctuations for $b<1$ via structure factor comparisons.
paper_structure: The paper develops the mathematical framework by introducing the warped rule, deriving the resulting bias, and then applying this framework to a 1D quantum gas model, comparing results across different ensemble averaging methods.
why_interesting: It provides a deep, non-trivial link between the fundamental postulates of quantum measurement (the Born rule) and macroscopic thermodynamic behavior (entropy extraction and phase ordering), which is highly relevant to non-equilibrium statistical mechanics.
